title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Use Bloom's taxonomy as a map of where 'being critical' sits, from remembering to creating.

title: A ladder, not a single step
body: So far this lesson has talked about 'being critical' as one habit. It is worth seeing where that habit actually sits on a wider ladder of thinking, so you can notice when you are only at the bottom of it.

title: Six rungs
body: Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised taxonomy sets out six levels of thinking: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, and create. Being critical mostly lives in the top three: breaking a claim down (analyse), judging it against others (evaluate), and building something new from what you have judged (create). This is a preview of the ladder, not a test of it; you will practise analyse and evaluate properly in later lessons.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students who have each just read the same journal article.

{{learner-a}} reads a source and can recite its main claim back accurately. That is remembering and understanding, useful, but it stops there.

{{learner-b}} reads the same source, then breaks its claim into the evidence it rests on and checks that evidence against another source. That is moving up the ladder into analysis and evaluation.

Both understood the article. Only {{learner-b}} had moved up the ladder.

title: Why the ladder matters for a habit of mind
body: A habit of mind is not a one-off climb. The point is to notice, every time, which rung you are actually on, and to make moving up it automatic rather than something you only do when a task tells you to.

definition: To break a claim, source or data set down into its parts in order to examine how it works or what it rests on.
extendedDefinition: In Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised taxonomy, 'analyse' sits above 'understand' and below 'evaluate': you are expected to take something apart, not just restate it.
example: Analysing a claim means asking what evidence it is built on, not just what the claim itself says.

title: Order the six levels
displayTitle: Put Bloom's six levels in order
body: These six levels of thinking, from Anderson and Krathwohl (2001), are listed out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the six levels of the revised taxonomy in order, from the most basic to the most demanding.

_feedback.correct: That is the correct order, from remembering a fact up to creating something new from your own judgement of it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which level has to come before another: you cannot evaluate something you have not yet analysed.

title: Noticing your own rung
body: Next time you read something for a task, pause and ask which rung you are actually on. If you can only restate the claim, you are not critical about it yet, whatever else the task required.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of something you read this week. Which rung of the ladder were you actually on, honestly?
What would it take to move one rung higher next time, without it taking much longer?
